summary: Systematic Investor series. Brennan splits trend followers into idiosyncratic (single-market) and correlation-conscious (cross-sectional) styles and links their relative fortunes to the globalization/deglobalization regime; he then covers futures data hygiene (back-adjustment, roll logic, proxies for micro contracts), minimum capital for retail trend following, and LLM pitfalls in strategy development.

coverage.note: intro, sponsor disclaimers, Japanese pen-tracking gadget (no method content)
AQR adopts machine learning; trend drawdowns; definition of idiosyncratic vs correlation-conscious trend
two tribes of trend: idiosyncratic versus correlation-conscious, history and regimes
April 2025 tariff whipsaw; debt and yields; drawdown length
multiple reversals, size and sector tilt, ensemble diversification, index returns
dynamic risk budgeting, is trend dead, teaser for data topics
democratization of retail futures trading, micro and nano contracts
nano fees, trends persist, why futures data and back-adjusting matter
Panama method, roll trigger, CSI data
adjustment bias in indicators, roll logic, survivorship, granularity
limited history of new contracts, proxies, tick scaling
scaling ladder of markets with capital, AI segment starts
LLM limits: plausible text not causality, generic indicator stitching
LLM mass optimization, hindsight bias, blind debugging, Claude Opus 4 anecdote
AI-risk anecdotes (Tudor Jones, Musk robots), closing; nothing actionable

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: AQR had better get a good reason for why the industry is going into their draw downs because we we're deep in our draw downs at the moment
claims.claim: Trend followers were in deep drawdowns in spring 2025, with the SG Trend Index touching or slightly exceeding its worst monthly drawdown in history.
claims.testable: yes: index drawdown is observable

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: The article mentioned that the shift has so far it's obviously a short time period uh improved returns but he also acknowledges uh Cliff that there are some drawbacks and that is how do you explain poor performance to investors?
claims.claim: AQR now uses machine learning to find market patterns even when the reason is unclear, which may help returns but makes poor performance hard to explain to investors; trend followers prefer knowing why they are long or short.
claims.testable: no: opinion about explainability

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: those that treat each individual market as independent and they're looking at time series momentum in an individual market
claims.claim: Idiosyncratic trend followers treat each market as independent and trade time-series momentum market by market, the traditional cut-losses-short approach of the 70s to 90s.
claims.testable: yes: separable from cross-sectional trend in a backtest

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: the correlation conscious segment those that treat trend following more in a cross-sectional viewpoint. They're looking at groupings, asset classes, complexes, um things that are trending.
claims.claim: Correlation-conscious trend followers look at groupings, asset classes and complexes (cross-sectional view) and manage portfolio correlation and volatility targeting; the industry split into these two styles in the early 2000s.
claims.testable: yes: the two styles can be implemented and compared

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: They reduced their volatility. there was a significant attempt to reduce volatility and in that process um they looked at how do they reduce volatility
claims.claim: Large trend managers cut target volatility from about 25% to 10-12% in the early 2000s to attract institutional assets, using correlation reduction and vol targeting, which smoothed returns at the cost of the two-way volatility of the classic style.
claims.testable: yes: vol target is a parameter

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: post um 2008 and I attributed that to a particular regime that was in place in globalization central bank coordination
claims.claim: Correlation-conscious trend following did very well from 2008 to 2020 because globalization and coordinated central bank policy made markets more causally correlated, which cross-sectional grouping could exploit.
claims.conditions: works in a globalized, centrally coordinated regime
claims.testable: partly: regime dating is subjective

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: I saw that the rise again of the idiosyncratic trend follower from 2020 up to 2024 and I saw a a a reduced performance of what I call a correlation conscious trend follower over that period
claims.claim: After 2020 deglobalization, fragmentation and loss of central bank coordination made assets less correlated, favouring idiosyncratic trends (cocoa, soybeans, gold) and hurting the large correlation-conscious managers.
claims.direction: favor idiosyncratic single-market trend over cross-sectional grouping
claims.testable: partly: compare the two styles by subperiod

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: I'm associating that with the tariff policies. I'm associating that with the fact that these tariff policies were so widespread in their impact.
claims.claim: April 2025 tariff announcements hit equities, commodities and currencies at once and caused massive whipsaws for all trend followers; the speaker expects this regime not to last because a direction must emerge.
claims.testable: no: view about a policy episode

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: what happens in in in this world if if 10 year interest rates settle above 5% and 75% is kind of your low point rather than zero
claims.claim: Rising global debt, weak bond auctions in Japan and the US and a 10-year yield that may settle above 5% mean institutions built portfolios for the old regime; when cracks appear trends can emerge with follow-through.
claims.conditions: trends follow once policy cracks appear
claims.testable: partly: yield level is observable, outcome is a view

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's a draw down that's now running at 12 14 months but that in itself is not unusual uh frankly
claims.claim: A 12-14 month trend-following drawdown is not unusual, and 2-3 months of strong follow-through in a few sectors can recover it.
claims.testable: yes: drawdown durations can be measured historically

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: all three big financial sectors currencies bonds and um and equities they have all had significant reversals but also multiple reversals
claims.claim: The 2024-25 drawdown was unusual because currencies, bonds and equities all reversed several times, which is the worst case for trend following in financial sectors.
claims.testable: yes: count trend reversals by sector

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the size have meant that they had to tilt the risk towards financial markets rather than commodities
claims.claim: Very large managers must tilt risk to liquid financial futures rather than commodities, losing diversification, which may explain why big established firms had their worst drawdowns.
claims.direction: commodities give diversification for smaller managers
claims.testable: partly: need manager-level sector risk data

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: you might have 500 600 return streams comprising say 60 70 markets but 10 uncorrelated trend following systems to create 600 return streams
claims.claim: Diversify with a system ensemble: about 10 structurally uncorrelated trend systems across 60-70 markets (500-600 return streams) rather than just adding correlated markets, because market correlations change quickly with politics.
claims.testable: yes: measure correlation among system return streams

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: trading hundreds of markets versus trading maybe 70 or 80 that are less correlated and maybe a a better bet for your portfolio than just trading you know hundreds of markets which eventually will be much highly correlated
claims.claim: Trading 70-80 less correlated markets may be a better bet than hundreds of eventually highly correlated markets.
claims.testable: yes: compare diversification versus market count

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: my trend barometer stood at 36. So, still a little bit, uh, weak and and therefore we are still seeing, you know, some challenging um environment for for for trend following
claims.claim: A trend barometer reading of 36 (weak) goes with a challenging environment for trend following.
claims.testable: yes: barometer readings vs subsequent trend returns

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the Btop 50 is up 48 basis points, down only 4% for the year now. Sockchen CTA index also up about 43 basis points. It's down about 8% for the year.
claims.claim: Early June 2025 data: BarclayHedge BTOP50 -4% YTD, SG CTA index -8%, SG Trend about -11%, short-term traders -3%, MSCI World +6.3%, S&P 500 total return +2%.
claims.indicator: BTOP50, SG CTA, SG Trend, SG Short Term Traders index returns
claims.testable: yes: published index figures

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I imagine um that actually risk budgeting has been quite dynamic the last couple of months meaning that we've actually seen big changes in the overall risk of CTAs.
claims.claim: Repeated reversals forced much more dynamic risk budgeting in spring 2025, with big swings in total CTA risk rather than the usual gradual change.
claims.testable: partly: needs CTA risk exposure data

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: maybe trend following is more relevant today than it's ever been because there's no logic in many of the things that is happening in the world
claims.claim: Trend following is still relevant because policy breaks will eventually produce trends a long/short manager can capture; the argument that markets have changed and trend is dead recurs in every drawdown.
claims.testable: no: belief about the future

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: mini contracts, micro contracts and in some cases what we call nano contracts
claims.claim: Mini, micro and nano futures (about 1/10, 1/100, 1/1000 of a standard lot) plus institutional-grade software let retail traders reach the diversification once needing $1-2 million.
claims.testable: no: market-structure observation

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: do brokers/ exchanges charge the same fee for a nano as that?
claims.claim: Fixed per-contract commissions hurt small contracts: $5 each way on a nano costs far more relative to notional than on a standard contract at the same number of round turns; percentage fees scaled to lot size fix this.
claims.indicator: commission per round turn vs contract size
claims.testable: yes: cost model per contract size

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: I believe in complex adaptive systems and um trends are an inherent nature of complex adaptive systems.
claims.claim: Trends will persist because they are an inherent property of complex adaptive systems, although the participants in trend following will change.
claims.testable: no: philosophical premise

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: If you back test the the raw data contracts, the gaps between the contracts are illusions and result in false signals if you don't adjust them.
claims.claim: Unadjusted stitched futures contracts contain artificial jumps at each roll that create false signals, so continuous back-adjusted series are required and should be built by the researcher.
claims.testable: yes: compare signals on raw versus adjusted data

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: the price of the front contract remains as is but you adjust the prior contracts to that every time you've got a new contract emerging
claims.claim: The Panama (difference) method keeps the current contract price and subtracts each roll gap from all earlier history, so the history must be re-adjusted at every new roll and early prices can turn negative in backwardation.
claims.testable: yes: implementable and checkable

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: you need to define a consistent roll trigger. In other words, do you use open interest in the next contract or do you use volume or do you use the calendar to decide when to roll?
claims.claim: Define one consistent roll trigger (open interest, volume or calendar) and observe the price gap at the roll to compute the adjustment.
claims.indicator: roll trigger: open interest, volume or calendar
claims.testable: yes: roll rule is a parameter

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: there is a very I would say inexpensive solution uh from a company in the US that have been doing this since the 70s and uh I think are known for having very clean data and that's CSI data
claims.claim: CSI Data is named as a low-cost, clean futures data source with user-selectable roll and adjustment methods.
claims.testable: no: vendor recommendation

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: So you've got to avoid things that adopt absolute price thresholds. For instance, buy if crude is greater than $100 or sell if gold is less than $1,500.
claims.claim: Because back-adjustment shifts historical price levels, avoid rules based on absolute price thresholds, long lookback percent returns, mean reversion to long averages and fixed dollar stops; use indicators agnostic to adjustment bias.
claims.testable: yes: test signal sensitivity to adjustment method

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: If you have a different roll logic, you're going to get a different
claims.claim: Backtest roll logic must match live roll logic, otherwise backtest and live results diverge.
claims.testable: yes: compare results under two roll rules

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: You've got to try and use data that uh shows these delisted contracts, shows the dead symbols.
claims.claim: Futures backtests suffer survivorship bias when delisted contracts and dead symbols are omitted, so use data including them.
claims.testable: yes: compare universes with and without dead contracts

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: using daily data when your signals are executed intraday
claims.claim: Data granularity must match execution: with only daily open-high-low-close data, rules should act only on those points and not infer positions between them.
claims.testable: yes: compare daily versus intraday execution

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: Your back test environment is where you stress test your models. Determine where they break.
claims.claim: A backtest should stress test models and find where they break, not estimate future returns; aim for robustness across regimes rather than curve fitting to one regime or market.
claims.testable: partly: robustness criteria are definable

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: you look on for instance something like CSI data for a standard contract of that same market that exists on the same exchange and hopefully has a similar price structure
claims.claim: For new micro/nano contracts with about three years of data, extend history with a proxy: the standard contract on the same exchange with similar price structure (scaled for tick size and tick value), and backtest on 20-40 years of that.
claims.indicator: standard contract as proxy for micro contract
claims.testable: yes: proxy and scaling are explicit

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: you can either overlap um splicing that that's where you have two contracts traded side by side for a period of time
claims.claim: Alternative to proxies: overlap-based or normalization-based splicing of two similar series; try proxies first.
claims.testable: yes: standard technique

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: $200,000 is basically what I'd regard as the minimum capital you need to adopt a suitable trend following process that gives a degree of diversification
claims.claim: Roughly $200,000 is the minimum capital for a diversified retail trend program using micro/mini/nano futures, with enough skin in the game for discipline.
claims.testable: partly: sizing granularity can be simulated

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: They diversify as far as they can and they fragment their risk with too much diversification and um with that limited set of capital you cannot position size correctly
claims.claim: Trap one: with small capital, over-diversifying across 100 markets makes it impossible to size equal risk per bet, leaving hidden correlation and risk of ruin.
claims.testable: yes: simulate position rounding at small capital

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: with levels of capital of about $200,000 you can comfortably allocate into about 10 uncorrelated markets. You can have five ensemble systems and you can deploy ATRbased normalization
claims.claim: At $200k run about 10 uncorrelated markets with 5 ensemble systems and ATR-based equal-risk sizing, then widen to about 30 markets at $400k and 60 markets at $1 million, adding standard contracts.
claims.testable: yes: define and simulate the scaling ladder

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: they're actually pattern recognizing statistical models that predict plausible text. They predict plausible text, not the causal relationships.
claims.claim: Large language models predict plausible text, not causal relationships, so strategies they propose look polished but lack robustness under stress and overfit.
claims.testable: partly: LLM-generated strategies can be backtested out of sample

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: I asked Chat GPT for a crude oil trading system. It gave me an SMA crossover with an RSA or RSI and ATR filters.
claims.claim: An LLM asked for a crude oil system returned a forum-favourite SMA crossover with RSI and ATR filters, not based on oil's volatility regime, seasonality or term structure, so it only works because it is tuned to past conditions.
claims.indicator: SMA crossover with RSI and ATR filters
claims.testable: yes: backtest out of sample

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: Some traders use AI to generate hundreds of rule sets then auto back test them looking for alpha. But what's really happening there is this curve fitting on steroids.
claims.claim: Auto-generating hundreds of strategies with AI and backtesting them is mass data mining that produces false positives which die in live trading unless regime validation and structural filters are applied.
claims.testable: yes: multiple-testing correction measurable

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: You're asking AI to reverse engineer entries from known outcomes.
claims.claim: Feeding historical charts to an LLM and asking what entry would have worked creates hindsight bias; rules trained on known outcomes fail when uncertainty is real.
claims.testable: yes: enforce point-in-time information

claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
claims.quote: the model can check if your code runs but it can't tell you if your system is conceptually sound or if your exit logic destroys for instance your convexity
claims.claim: LLMs are useful for debugging syntax and porting code, but cannot judge whether a system is conceptually sound, for example whether exit logic destroys convexity; human validation with causal logic is needed.
claims.testable: no: judgement
